clue.text: College grounds acceptable in temporary quarters

indicators.note: the word in says the acceptable letter sits inside the temporary quarters

parts.note: camps are temporary living quarters, as for soldiers or scouts
U is the old shorthand for upper-class, so socially acceptable

explanation.surface: A university's grounds are passable as a stopgap place to live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts U inside CAMPS. U for 'acceptable' comes from the old British U and non-U labels for upper-class and not upper-class usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The grounds and buildings of a university or college form its site.

clue.text: So upset after tea with the utter confusion

indicators.note: after places the turned piece behind the drink in the finished word

parts.note: cha is British slang for tea

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word So is read bottom to top

explanation.surface: Someone is upset after tea, with everything in a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA is old British slang for tea, from Chinese. In a down clue 'upset' means turned bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Total disorder is a synonym for complete muddle.

clue.text: Headmaster to pay interest on this?

definitions.meaning: the head of a school or college
the capital sum of a loan, on which interest is charged

explanation.surface: A school head wonders whether he should be paying interest on something.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition plays on the money sense: the sum borrowed, as opposed to the interest charged on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A school's head teacher has this title; separately, a loan's capital sum, which earns interest, carries the same name.

clue.text: Sat around, main problem, staying power

indicators.note: around tells us the letters of Sat are moved about into a new order
problem suggests the letters of main are in trouble and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Sitting about, the chief difficulty is endurance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sat around' reads as lounging, but 'around' and 'problem' each scramble only the word before them.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance, the ability to keep going over a long effort.

clue.text: It is not bound to be of interest to readers

definitions.text: It is not bound to be of interest to readers

parts.words: It is not bound to be of interest to readers
parts.note: bound means fastened in covers like a book, not obliged: a thin unbound booklet written for readers

explanation.surface: Something is not necessarily going to appeal to its audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not bound to be' reads as 'not certain to be', but means 'not stitched into hard covers'.
explanation.definitionFit: A short unbound booklet or tract, printed for readers.

clue.text: Briefed about having been given a film role

definitions.text: having been given a film role
definitions.meaning: literally placed in a motion picture

explanation.surface: Someone was briefed about landing a part in a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is a link. The idiom for informing someone is read literally as casting them in a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means informed of the situation; literally it means cast in a movie.

clue.text: Prohibit non-alcoholic drink first in café!

indicators.note: first places the drink at the front, ahead of the word for prohibit

parts.note: milk is a drink with no alcohol
to bar is to forbid

explanation.surface: A café owner bans any soft drink being served first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' puts MILK ahead of BAR. In Britain a milk bar was a snack bar serving milk drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A snack counter serving milkshakes and light food is a kind of eatery.

clue.text: Part of book allowed to be circular

parts.note: a leaf is a single sheet of a book
let means permitted

explanation.surface: Part of a book was permitted to go round in a loop.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular is a printed notice handed out widely, a flyer.

clue.text: The Marines and I would otherwise have a month in France

parts.note: taken as written
RM stands for Royal Marines
I'd is the short form of I would
or means otherwise, as in hurry or you'll miss it

explanation.surface: Soldiers and a speaker plan to spend a month in France.
explanation.walkthrough: THERMIDOR was the eleventh month of the French Revolutionary calendar, roughly late July to August.
explanation.definitionFit: In the French Revolutionary calendar, the summer period of heat was named this.

clue.text: Large area for potentially fair accountant

indicators.note: potentially says the letters of fair could be rearranged into something else

parts.note: CA is chartered accountant

explanation.surface: A big region might be a fair job for an accountant.
explanation.walkthrough: CA, chartered accountant, is a common British professional abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A continent is a very large landmass, which fits a large area.

clue.text: Put up with new role in the gallery

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters inside the name of the gallery

parts.note: the Tate is the famous London art gallery

indicators.note: new signals the letters of role are made into a fresh order

explanation.surface: An artist puts up with a new job in the gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the London art gallery; 'new' scrambles only 'role'.
explanation.definitionFit: To endure or bear something is a synonym of the phrasal verb.

clue.text: Justification for penalty imposed

definitions.meaning: official approval or authorisation for an action
a measure taken to punish, as against a country

explanation.surface: A reason is given for a penalty being enforced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is a link. The word means both permission and its near opposite, a punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both official approval and a punitive measure, a famous contradictory pair.

clue.text: Wrongly blamed for the pandemonium

indicators.note: wrongly suggests the letters of blamed are set out in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone was unfairly accused of causing the chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrongly' rearranges BLAMED. The answer is the old name of a London asylum, now meaning uproar.
explanation.definitionFit: Uproar and wild chaos, from the name of a notorious hospital for the insane.

clue.text: Stroke of punishment causing injury?

definitions.meaning: a neck injury from a sudden jolt

explanation.surface: A punishing blow causes harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Causing' is a link. The first definition reads the answer literally as a lash of a whip.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a lash from a whip; also a neck sprain suffered in car crashes.

clue.text: Having beaten the German before outbreak of flu — that's marvellous

parts.note: won means having beaten an opponent
der is a German word for the

indicators.note: outbreak suggests the letters of flu burst out of order

explanation.surface: A victory over the German, just before flu breaks out, is splendid news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outbreak of' reads as illness spreading but scrambles the flu letters. 'Before' and 'that's' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean excellent or wonderful-seeming, a synonym pair.

clue.text: Was at ease in the wild desert

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of desert are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Someone relaxed out in the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges DESERT. 'In the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To have relaxed or reposed is to have been at ease.

clue.text: Sweetbread?

parts.note: read as a sweet loaf: a cone of hard refined sugar shaped like a loaf, not the offal

explanation.surface: A diner asks about offal.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweetbread is an organ meat, but split it reads 'sweet bread', a loaf made of sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Refined sugar was once sold as a hard cone, a loaf of sweetness.

clue.text: Central parts in clue reconstruction

indicators.note: reconstruction says the letters of clue and in are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A setter rebuilds a clue around its central parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reconstruction' rearranges CLUE and IN together.
explanation.definitionFit: Cores, the central parts of atoms or cells; plural to match parts.

clue.text: Rude song heard coming from the ship

indicators.note: heard says the words for rude and song are taken by their sound

parts.note: coarse means rude and an air is a song

explanation.surface: A bawdy tune is overheard coming from a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: COARSE AIR spoken sounds like the answer. 'Coming from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirate vessel, especially of the Barbary coast, so a kind of vessel.

clue.text: Singers turned at the entrance

indicators.note: turned suggests the letters of Singers are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Choir members turned round at the doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned' rearranges SINGERS. 'At the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Going in, or a way in; a formal synonym for entry.

clue.text: Theatre attendant?

parts.note: not an usher on the staff but someone who attends the theatre as audience

explanation.surface: A question about the staff in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attendant' suggests a member of staff, but here it means one who attends.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who regularly goes to see stage shows.

clue.text: Salt and vinegar

parts.note: not a crisp flavour: a chemical salt formed from the acid in vinegar

explanation.surface: A packet of crisps flavoured with salt and vinegar.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the British crisp flavour; the answer is a salt of acetic acid, the acid in vinegar.
explanation.definitionFit: A salt or ester of acetic acid, the acid that gives vinegar its sharpness.

clue.text: Are about to scold the little creature

indicators.note: about says the letters of Are are moved round

parts.note: wig is an old verb meaning to scold, as in wigging

explanation.surface: People are about to tell off a small animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are about to' reads as one phrase but splits into an anagram and a synonym. To wig is old British slang for to scold.
explanation.definitionFit: A small insect with pincers is a little creature.

clue.text: Making a space in the forest

definitions.text: Making a space in the forest

parts.words: Making a space in the forest
parts.note: both the act of removing trees and the open glade that results

explanation.surface: Someone is cutting a gap among the trees.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means removing obstacles and also an open treeless patch in woodland.

clue.text: Reflect on heartless girl in square

indicators.note: heartless means the middle of girl is removed, leaving its first and last letters

parts.note: a T-square is a drawing tool, so T can stand for square

explanation.surface: Someone reflects on a cold-hearted girl in a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' leaves GL from GIRL; IN is given as written; T is from T-square. 'On' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To flash or gleam with reflected light.

clue.text: Female youngster by the water in France has a torch

parts.note: a lamb is a young sheep
eau is French for water

explanation.surface: A girl by the waterside in France carries a torch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A flaming torch, from the French for a lit wick.

clue.text: A US soldier catches out the rodent

indicators.note: catches means the soldier holds the next word within him

parts.note: GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: An American soldier traps a rodent.
explanation.walkthrough: GI is the standard name for an American soldier. 'The' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical American burrowing animal related to the guinea pig.

clue.text: Generosity from Scotland's capital, say

indicators.note: say signals that the description is taken by its sound

parts.note: the capital letter of Scotland is a large S

explanation.surface: Generosity is said to come from Edinburgh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like Edinburgh, but means the first letter, a capital or large S; said out loud, 'large S' gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lavish giving of money or gifts, a synonym of liberality.

clue.text: One must try hard to make it

definitions.text: One must try hard to make it

parts.words: One must try hard to make it
parts.note: the clue describes the thing produced by trying hard, an attempt or exertion

explanation.surface: Advice that success needs determination.
explanation.definitionFit: An exertion or strenuous attempt is what trying hard produces.
